paper_title: Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Long-horizon terminal agents may solve a task in one run yet fail across repeated runs. Stochastic errors can propagate through actions and context, creating a gap between capability and reliable execution. We present RiseHarness, a framework for iteratively improving agent harnesses with model weights fixed. It focuses on flipping tasks with both successful and failed runs under the same configuration, using successful runs as references for failure analysis. RiseHarness combines agent trajectories with internal harness traces from a runtime monitor to examine how model actions interact with command execution, feedback, context management, and completion decisions. A Harness Handbook links this evidence to harness behaviors and source code, helping identify recurring problems in mechanisms shared across tasks. RiseHarness then searches other harness frameworks for relevant implementations and adapts them as design references to the current model and execution protocol. Candidate changes undergo behavioral checks and repeated task evaluation; versions with measured gains seed the next iteration. This loop integrates suitable mechanisms from different frameworks into a single harness and uses new execution evidence to guide further changes. We evaluate task success and reliability across models, ablate harness execution evidence and external research, and test transfer to unseen benchmarks with the same model. RiseHarness treats a specific model as the unit of harness adaptation, studying how changes to shared interaction mechanisms can make existing capabilities more reliable across tasks.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: A model that solves long-horizon terminal task once may fail to do so consistently. Across many interactions, an incorrect command or missed observation can change the environment and the context available for later decisions. Stochastic generation can therefore lead to diﬀerent outcomes even when the task and model remain unchanged. Long-horizon terminal benchmarks examine workﬂows requiring hundreds of interactions and sustained progress [1, 2]. This distinction between reaching successful outcome and succeeding reliably across repeated runs is central to agent evaluation [3, 4]. We study how to narrow this gap by improving the harness around ﬁxed model. Training-based approaches improve terminal agents through reinforcement learning and veriﬁed task synthesis [5, 6]. The harness controls command execution, observation feedback, context management, and completion decisions. Interface design can aﬀect agent performance without updating model weights [7], and the harness itself has become target for automatic improvement. Execution traces and evaluation feedback can guide changes to harness code and support the evaluation of their eﬀects [810]. Failure-informed runtime 1 interventions have also been studied as way to improve repeated success without changing model weights [11]. Our focus is how to connect diﬀerences between successful and failed runs to actual internal harness behavior, identify shared mechanisms to improve, and use implementations from other frameworks as references for changes suited to the current harness and model. diﬀerence between two trajectories does not by itself establish that harness behavior is missing: the harness may already provide the relevant feedback, or the information needed for proposed intervention may not be available. Likewise, an eﬀective design in another framework may depend on diﬀerent interfaces or execution conditions. We introduce RiseHarness, which uses execution evidence to check these conditions and to design and validate changes. With the evaluated model held ﬁxed, its evolution loop combines comparisons of successful and failed runs, internal execution analysis, and research into existing implementations. We begin with ﬂipping tasks, which have both successful and failed runs under the same model and harness conﬁguration. Successful runs show that the current system can solve the task and provide references for analyzing failures. Same-task trajectory contrast and cross-task aggregation help identify recurring behavioral In RiseHarness, the contrast ﬁrst identiﬁes behavioral need; the analysis then checks problems [12]. whether the current harness can support that behavior and whether it already performs it. runtime monitor records internal execution and aligns these harness traces with agent trajectories, exposing how proposed actions are dispatched and how feedback reaches the model. We use the Harness Handbook [13] to connect these records to behavioral responsibilities and implementing code. This joint analysis helps distinguish an agents unsuccessful response from missing or ineﬀective harness mechanism and groups supported ﬁndings into targets for shared changes. External documentation can inform the implementation of agent capabilities [14]. RiseHarness searches other frameworks, source code, and technical documentation for implementations relevant to the behavioral problems identiﬁed through execution analysis. For completion decisions, for example, it can examine how other frameworks track unﬁnished commands or verify results. The system studies the signals and interfaces these designs require, then considers the current harnesss execution ﬂow, available information, and model behavior to decide which ideas are applicable and how to modify existing mechanisms. The goal is to draw on useful designs from diﬀerent frameworks to develop harness whose mechanisms work together for the current model. Behavioral checks assess whether candidate implements the intended change, while repeated task evaluations measure its eﬀect on performance. Accepted changes provide the basis for subsequent rounds; unsuccessful candidates supply execution evidence for revising the implementation or proposed mechanism. Model weights remain ﬁxed throughout. RiseHarness evolves the harness for speciﬁc model based on its execution behavior. Models may require diﬀerent forms of interaction support [15, 16]; we therefore conduct evolution separately for each model and examine the resulting behavioral changes. These changes aﬀect shared mechanisms for command execution, observation feedback, and completion. Their beneﬁts beyond the evolution tasks require separate validation. Repeated evaluations and ablations assess the eﬀects on task success and execution reliability, as well as the contributions of dual-trace evidence and research into external implementations. We then hold both the model and the evolved harness ﬁxed and evaluate on benchmarks not used for evolution to test whether these behavioral improvements support broader range of tasks. Our main contributions are: An evidence-driven harness evolution framework. We introduce RiseHarness, which uses successful runs as references for failed runs and iteratively retains harness changes that improve measured performance without updating model weights. Behavioral diagnosis from paired runs and internal execution. We combine agent and harness traces with the Harness Handbook to check proposed behavioral needs against actual execution and locate shared 2 Figure 1 Operations within discovery round of RiseHarness: record dual traces, identify shared behavioral problems, research and adapt mechanisms, and implement and evaluate changes. The Handbook connects execution evidence to harness behavior and code. mechanisms for modiﬁcation. Harness modiﬁcation informed by external implementations. We retrieve relevant implementations from other frameworks, examine their requirements, and use the current harnesss structure, runtime signals, and model behavior to design speciﬁc changes. Reliability and generalization. Repeated runs and ablations assess harness evidence and external research; we compare changes across models and test cross-benchmark transfer with the model held ﬁxed.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Long-horizon execution and success consistency. Long-horizon agents must coordinate reasoning, actions, and execution feedback across many interactions [17, 18]. Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench and its 2.0 extension use intermediate grading to measure progress through extended workﬂows [1, 2]. Local errors can alter the environment and subsequent context, leading to diﬀerent outcomes for the same model and task. Average success alone therefore does not fully capture execution reliability. τ -bench measures consistency through passk, the proportion of tasks solved in all repeated trials [3]; broader reliability research also examines robustness, predictability, and safety [4]. AgentDebug diagnoses errors and supplies corrective feedback for recovery [19]; AgentRx localizes failures using constraints and evidence-bearing validation logs [20]. FIRE studies failure-informed runtime interventions that improve repeated success without updating model weights [11]. These studies motivate examining whether an agent system can consistently support successful execution, beyond whether its model can solve task at all. We study tasks with both successful and failed runs to assess whether harness changes can narrow this gap. Agent harnesses. The harness is the runtime layer that organizes modelenvironment interaction, including command execution, observation construction, context management, and completion decisions. SWE-agent shows that interface design aﬀects task performance with ﬁxed model [7]. OpenHands provides composable tools, memory management, sandboxed execution, and lifecycle control, illustrating the components of this layer [21]. Memory, planning, and action modules also appear in agentic recommender architectures [22]. Understanding how harness aﬀects execution requires both runtime observations and knowledge of its implementation. HarnessBank and HarnessDev further show that the eﬀects of harness changes can depend on the runtime model [15, 16]. Harness design thus requires understanding both its internal mechanisms and how the model responds to them. Harness self-evolution. Automated agent design optimizes prompts, workﬂows, and executable agents [24 28]. Iterative response reﬁnement is also studied in federated in-context learning and uncertainty-aware reasoning [29, 30]. Veriﬁed trajectory rewriting and recursive policy reﬁnement improve terminal models through training [31, 32]. AHE, HarnessFix, and Meta-Harness use execution evidence and evaluation feedback to guide harness updates [810]. ModularRSI contrasts successful and failed runs, aggregates ﬁndings across tasks, and evolves modular components [12]. Self-Harness analyzes failures and retains ﬁxed-model edits through regression tests [33]. HarnessEvolve also uses successful references for failure analysis, but generates and veriﬁes them with access to ground-truth answers [34]. Related work explores design reuse [35], external documentation [14], and controls against benchmark overﬁtting [36]. Evaluation studies also emphasize matched-budget search baselines and held-out tests [37]. Our framework combines same-conﬁguration successes, dual traces, and the Handbook to check behavioral needs, then consults external implementations to design local changes. Candidates undergo implementation checks and repeated evaluation; transfer is assessed separately with the harness held ﬁxed.

sections.title: 3 Harness Self-Evolution
sections.content: RiseHarness is harness self-evolution framework for long-horizon agents. It uses execution evidence and external design knowledge to iteratively improve execution reliability while keeping model weights ﬁxed. We ﬁrst introduce the basic concepts and notation in the preliminaries. We then describe the four components of the methodexecution recording and behavior localization, problem discovery and grouping, mechanism research and adaptation, and implementation and validationwith reference to Figure 1 and Algorithm 1.

Modiﬁcations are conﬁned to harness prompts and executable interaction logic; the model proposing them may diﬀer from Mθ. At round t, the current harness Ht has corresponding Handbook Kt and reference corpus Rt containing outcomes and dual traces from rt 2 complete repetitions per task. The initial corpus R0 is collected by repeatedly running the seed harness H0 on D. The ﬁnding set is partitioned into behavioral groups G: ﬁndings in one group could be addressed by shared harness change. Each ﬁnding belongs to one group, while single run pair may yield several ﬁndings assigned to diﬀerent groups. The selected groups are denoted by Gt G. sections.title: 3.2 Execution Evidence
sections.content: Improving harness ﬁrst requires distinguishing the models requested actions from the systems actual behavior. An agent trajectory τ agent records the information the model receives, its responses, and tool interactions, but does not fully expose internal harness processing. requested command, for example, may not be dispatched, and terminal output may not be returned to the model in full. The agent trajectory alone may therefore be insuﬃcient to locate the problem. RiseHarness uses runtime monitor to record calling relationships, arguments, return values, exceptions, and source locations at selected harness function boundaries, producing harness trace τ harness. Run identiﬁers and episode indices link the two traces, allowing the analysis to follow model request through its processing and the feedback ultimately returned. Both traces, together with task outcomes and execution identities, are retained in the reference corpus Rt. Function-level records must also be connected to behavior. Because single harness behavior may span several functions, RiseHarness uses Handbook Kt aligned with the current source to describe behavioral responsibilities, triggers, implementing functions, and exit conditions [13]. These mappings connect individual calls to command execution, observation handling, context management, and completion checks. They explain each calls role in the overall mechanism and help locate the relevant code. The traces thus establish what happened, while the Handbook identiﬁes the behavior involved and its implementation. For pair p, the paired agent and harness traces pa and ph provide execution evidence. The Handbook Kt connects these records to harness behavior during analysis (line 5) and supports mechanism adaptation during proposal generation (line 6). Initial seed runs supply R0; candidate screening and full evaluation use the same recording process (lines 1112), supplying new execution evidence for subsequent iterations.

sections.title: 3.3 Behavioral Analysis
sections.content: This stage identiﬁes behavioral problems in repeated runs and groups related ﬁndings into targets for harness improvement. We focus on ﬂipping tasks, which have both successful and failed runs under the same model 5 and harness conﬁguration. Successful runs show that the current system can complete the task and provide concrete references for examining failures. Let yi,j(Ht) {0, 1} indicate whether task succeeds in repetition under harness Ht. The ﬂipping task set in Rt is 8 < :i : 0 < rtX j= Ft = 9 = ; . yi,j(Ht) < rt (1) For each ﬂipping task, the system pairs successful and failed runs, examines relevant interactions, and uses their execution diﬀerences to formulate behavioral wishes. Each wish is checked against the information available to the harness and the mechanisms it actually executed at the time. Findings from individual pairs are then pooled to identify shared behavioral needs across tasks. Four operations implement this process (Algorithm 1, lines 56):

sections.title: Group
sections.content: Compare relevant interactions, identify execution diﬀerences, and use the Handbook to interpret the harnesss role. Use comparison evidence and agent traces to specify what the harness should do and under which observable conditions. Inspect harness traces to assess whether the required information was available and the existing mechanism had already performed the behavior; revise the wish accordingly. Pool ﬁndings across pairs, group those that could be addressed by shared behavioral change, and formulate common wish. The ﬁrst three operations produce the ﬁnding set A, retaining revised wishes, assessments, and supporting evidence. single run pair may expose several problems and therefore yield ﬁndings assigned to diﬀerent groups. After grouping, an independent review checks whether each common wish applies to all members and whether the groups correspond to distinct modiﬁcation needs. Review feedback guides regrouping. Groups that remain disputed or are excluded by the history do not proceed to proposal generation. The remaining groups are ranked by distinct-task coverage, distinct failing runs, and ﬁnding count to select Gt. Each selected group carries its common wish and complete member evidence into the next stage of mechanism research and design.

sections.title: 3.4 Design Exploration
sections.content: This stage turns shared behavioral wishes into concrete harness modiﬁcation proposals. Given the selected groups Gt, current harness Ht, Handbook Kt, and reference corpus Rt, Propose examines implementations in other frameworks to generate proposals Pt (line 6). The system ﬁrst uses group evidence, the Handbook, and source code to identify the behavior to improve, its current implementation, and the available runtime information. It then translates the common wish into search questions. The search examines how other harnesses handle similar problems, including their execution ﬂow, maintained state, and feedback to the model. For information loss in long command outputs, for example, it can investigate how full outputs are saved, key information is presented, and later retrieval is supported. Retrieved implementations and their sources are retained as references for designing local changes. The system then designs changes suited to the current harnesss structure, interaction protocol, and model behavior observed in the traces. Each design speciﬁes how the borrowed ideas would aﬀect existing mechanisms, where the required information would come from, and whether additional state or interface support is needed. The system also examines traces from tasks that succeeded in every recorded repetition to assess whether the proposed intervention could disrupt successful execution and to reﬁne its triggers and scope. 6 The resulting proposals specify behavioral changes, implementation sites, dependencies, and additional interaction costs, along with expected outcomes and observations for testing them. Each proposal links its execution evidence and external design sources for subsequent implementation and validation. If no suitable external precedent is found, the system retains the search record and may propose an explicitly identiﬁed local design.

sections.title: 3.5 Validation and Evolution
sections.content: Once proposals are generated, Implement applies them to the current harness Ht to build candidate Ct, together with its updated Handbook and trace recording conﬁguration (Algorithm 1, line 10). The system checks that the candidate can run and record traces. When enabled, independent behavioral checks (Appendix A.2) test whether each change produces the expected behavior under the speciﬁed conditions. Problems found during checking are fed back for repair within predeﬁned attempt limit. Only candidates that pass these checks proceed to task evaluation. Evaluation proceeds through screening followed by full validation. Screen examines task outcomes and mechanism activation on proposal-related tasks to select conﬁguration for validation. Evaluate then collects fresh repeated runs on the development set D, producing outcomes and dual traces Et (lines 1112). Adoption depends on this full evaluation: the records must be valid, the required run set complete, and the aggregate pass rate higher than the declared comparison baseline (line 14). On adoption, Publish saves the candidate and its Handbook as Ht+1 and Kt+1, and uses Et as the next reference corpus Rt+1 (line 15). Source code, mechanism settings, and recording conﬁguration are saved with the version, keeping the implementation, behavioral description, and execution evidence aligned for the next round. If the candidate is not adopted, the current version and its reference data are retained. Checking and evaluation records from each round are added to the history to guide subsequent search (line 17). Based on this evidence, the system decides whether to repair the implementation, revise proposal requirements, or try other proposals. Revisit returns existing proposals to the same implementation and validation process (line 8). After new version is adopted, discovery resumes with the updated execution evidence. Iteration ends at the round limit or another conﬁgured stopping condition.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: We evaluate RiseHarness across models to examine its eﬀects on task success and execution reliability in long-horizon terminal tasks. We use ablations to assess the contributions of key components and evaluate evolved harnesses on benchmarks not used for evolution to examine transfer. Section 4.1 describes the models, benchmarks, baselines, and evaluation protocol. The remaining subsections address the following four research questions: RQ1: Compared with the seed harness and existing baselines, can RiseHarness improve task success and repeated-run reliability across models? (Section 4.2) RQ2: How does removing harness traces and the Handbook, or omitting external design research, aﬀect harness evolution? (Section 4.3) RQ3: How do retained harness changes vary across models in their behavioral targets and intervention mechanisms? (Section 4.4) RQ4: With the model and evolved harness ﬁxed, do gains in task success and reliability transfer to benchmarks not used for evolution? (Section 4.4)

sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Models and benchmarks. We evaluate RiseHarness on GPT-6-sol and DeepSeek-V4-Flash, keeping model weights ﬁxed throughout harness evolution. For each model, we start from the unmodiﬁed Terminus-2 harness and evolve it on Terminal-Bench Hard (TBH), benchmark of 100 challenging terminal tasks described by Li et al. [31]. Repeated runs on TBH provide both execution trajectories for behavioral analysis and task outcomes for evaluating changes and selecting harness versions. To assess cross-benchmark generalization, we freeze the evolved harnesses and test them on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (TB2.1), which contains 89 tasks [38]. TB2.1 is used only for transfer evaluation and does not inform harness modiﬁcations. Baselines and evaluation protocol. We compare RiseHarness with the seed Terminus-2 harness, ModularRSI [12], and AHE Harness [9]. We also include two ablation baselines to assess the contributions of key components: RiseHarness w/o Harness Evidence: analysis uses only agent traces and source code, without harness traces or the Harness Handbook. RiseHarness w/o External Research: analysis retains dual traces and the Handbook, but proposals are generated from local information without external research. Full RiseHarness and both ablation baselines start from the same seed harness and reference runs, with matched models, editable scope, and predeﬁned budgets. Apart from the removed components, their procedures are identical (Section 4.3). We evaluate the publicly released ModularRSI harness without re-evolution. Each selected harness is frozen before independent repeated evaluation. The reference-baseline and versionselection rules used during evolution are speciﬁed in Appendices C.2 and C.3. Metrics and reporting. We measure both average task performance and repeated-run reliability. Unless otherwise stated, each task is evaluated in = 4 repeated runs. For task and repetition j, let yi,j(H) = 1 denote pass under harness and yi,j(H) = 0 scored failure. Scoring and completeness rules are speciﬁed in Appendix C.1. For task set S, we report four metrics, distinguishing average success from reliability across repeated runs [3]: Pass@1: the average pass rate over all tasks and repetitions, measuring performance in single run. Passr: the fraction of tasks that pass in all runs, measuring repeated-run success reliability. Pass@r: the fraction of tasks that pass at least once in runs, measuring observed task coverage within limited number of attempts. Flip: the fraction of tasks with both successful and failed runs, measuring outcome inconsistency. sections.title: 4.2 Performance and Reliability
sections.content: Overall performance. Table 1 summarizes task performance for RiseHarness and the comparison baselines. Relative to the seed Terminus-2 harness, RiseHarness improves both average success and repeated-run reliability across the two models, with higher Pass@1 and Pass4. For GPT-6-sol, RiseHarness improves Pass@1 by 5.25% and 3.09% on TBH and TB2.1, respectively, while increasing the all-success task fraction on both benchmarks. For DeepSeek-V4-Flash, RiseHarness improves TBH Pass@1 by 7.25% and Pass4 by 14%. Pass@4 increases only modestly in comparison, suggesting that the main gain is in repeated-run success reliability rather than large expansion in observed task coverage. Performance across iterations. Figures 2 and 3 show task outcome distributions and pass rates, respectively, as four mechanisms for completion conﬁrmation accumulate for DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Each version retains the preceding changes and adds one mechanism; their deﬁnitions and triggers appear in Appendix B. On TBH, despite ﬂuctuations among intermediate versions, the ﬁnal version achieves the highest average pass rate and all-success task fraction, while reducing both ﬂipping and all-failure tasks relative to the seed harness. Overall, the results show that RiseHarness improves success and reliability on the evolution tasks and also beneﬁts the same model on benchmark not used for evolution.

sections.title: 4.3 Component Contributions
sections.content: We use two ablations to examine the contributions of harness execution evidence and external design research to harness evolution for DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Apart from the removed component, the analysis, implementation, and evaluation procedures remain unchanged. Execution evidence. Figure 5 compares full RiseHarness with the variant without harness traces or the Handbook. The ablated variant retains access to agent traces and source code and follows the same external research procedure. On TBH, the full method achieves Pass@1 and Pass4 gains of 7% and 8%, respectively, indicating that harness traces and the Handbook provide useful information beyond agent traces and source code. On TB2.1, the full method also outperforms the ablated variant on both metrics, supporting the joint contribution of these two sources of information to the evolved harness. 10 Figure 7 Model-adapted vs. swapped ﬁnal harnesses (r = 4). GPT: GPT-6-sol; DeepSeek: DeepSeek-V4-Flash, using its ﬁnal + IR harness. Y-axes start above zero. External research. Figure 5 compares full RiseHarness with the variant that generates proposals using only local information. Both variants use dual traces and the Handbook; they diﬀer in whether they search for external designs and implementations. On TBH, the full method improves Pass@1 and Pass4 by 5.50% and 6%, respectively, while achieving higher Pass@4 and lower Flip. On TB2.1, the full method also maintains higher average success and all-success task fractions. These results suggest that external research usefully complements local execution analysis, with beneﬁts on both the evolution tasks and tasks not used for evolution.

sections.title: 4.4 Adaptation and Generalization
sections.content: Model-speciﬁc behavioral requirements. The retained changes diﬀer across models. DeepSeek-V4Flash strengthens the evidence required for completion, whereas GPT-6-sol emphasizes execution continuity and feedback through session recovery, workspace diﬀs, and prior-work evidence. Figure 4 locates these changes; Appendix describes their mechanisms. Figure 7 compares each models ﬁnal harness with the harness evolved for the other model. Both models perform better with their own harnesses on both benchmarks (full results in Appendix D.4). Cross-benchmark generalization. We freeze the harnesses evolved on TBH and evaluate them on TB2.1 with the execution model unchanged. Figure 6 compares performance with Terminus-2. Both models retain gains in average success and all-success task fraction on TB2.1; the direct transfer of DeepSeeks ﬁnal + IR version is reported in Appendix D.2. Together, the transfer experiments show that harness improvements can extend to unseen tasks while remaining sensitive to the model executing them.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented RiseHarness, framework that iteratively improves the harness to increase task success and execution reliability for long-horizon terminal agents while keeping model weights ﬁxed. Starting from ﬂipping tasks, it contrasts successful and failed runs under the same conﬁguration and combines agent trajectories, internal harness traces, and Harness Handbook to connect execution problems to speciﬁc It then searches other harness frameworks for relevant interaction behaviors and their implementations. designs and develops proposals suited to the current execution ﬂow, available signals, and model behavior. Implementation checks and repeated evaluation determine whether change is retained. Accepted versions, together with their updated Handbooks and execution evidence, become the basis for subsequent iterations. Our experiments show that harness evolution can improve average task performance and increase the fraction of tasks solved consistently across repeated runs. Ablations further support the contributions of harness execution evidence and external design research: the former exposes internal processing that agent trajectories alone may not reveal, while the latter provides design options beyond local analysis. The changes retained for 11 diﬀerent models target diﬀerent behaviors and use diﬀerent interventions. Swapping the evolved harnesses between models reduces performance, supporting model-speciﬁc harness adaptation. At the same time, frozen harnesses retain gains on benchmark not used for evolution, demonstrating the transfer value of improvements to interaction mechanisms shared across tasks. These ﬁndings show that systematic harness analysis and evolution can help models use their existing capabilities more reliably, alongside improvements to the models themselves. Future work will examine the approach across more models, task distributions, and agent frameworks, and explore ways to reduce the evaluation cost of harness evolution.

sections.title: A System Implementation
sections.content: This appendix supplements Sections 3.23.5 and Algorithm 1. Model-speciﬁc mechanisms, evaluation rules, and supplementary results follow in Appendices B, C, and D, respectively. Worked examples for both models and saved prompt excerpts appear in Sections A.4 and A.5. A.1 Evidence and Versioning Each reference corpus Rt contains task outcomes and paired agent and harness traces under the current harness Ht. Run identiﬁers and episode indices connect model requests to the internal calls that process them and the observations returned to the model. The monitor records selected function boundaries, including arguments, returns, exceptions, caller relationships, and source locations. The Handbook Kt maps these records to behavioral responsibilities and implementing functions. The two sources are complementary: traces describe observed execution, while the Handbook supplies the behavioral structure used to interpret it. candidate comprises source changes, mechanism settings, an updated Handbook, and compatible recording conﬁguration. Smoke checks establish that it can run and record traces. On adoption, these artifacts are saved together with the full evaluation outcomes and traces Et. They become the next harness, Handbook, and reference corpus, keeping subsequent analysis tied to the accepted implementation. Rejection preserves the current version. A.2 Behavioral Validation When independent behavioral checking is enabled, each implemented mechanism has contract describing its trigger conditions, observable eﬀects, relevant hooks and state, and runtime setting. Dependencies, replacements, and conﬂicts specify which mechanisms may be enabled together. These checks concern the implementation of proposed behavior; task evaluation measures its eﬀect on performance. Contracts include positive and negative cases and recovery cases where applicable. For an input x, let o(x) denote the expected incumbent behavior and o+(x) the expected modiﬁed behavior. An independent observer ﬁrst checks the incumbent expectation before the contract is frozen. The implementation is then checked in three conﬁgurations: O(Ht, x) = o(x), O(Ct, new mechanisms disabled, x) = o(x), O(Ct, mechanism and dependencies enabled, x) = o+(x). (3) The disabled conﬁguration checks preservation of incumbent behavior, while the enabled conﬁguration checks the intended intervention. Observed results are compared with the frozen expectations; process crash cannot establish successful handling of negative case. Failures are returned for repair within the conﬁgured attempt limit. These ﬁnite cases do not guarantee correctness on all tasks or isolate mechanism that executes with dependencies. A.3 Iteration Management Each round links proposals, checks, outcomes, and execution evidence to the candidate. The history guides implementation repair, proposal revision, alternative proposals, or renewed discovery after adoption. The proposing model may diﬀer from the ﬁxed evaluated model Mθ. The round limit and policy Π bound this process. Candidates must pass the conﬁgured checks before evaluation; adoption requires valid, complete full evaluation under the aggregate pass-rate rule in Appendix C.2. Screening alone cannot promote candidate. 16 A.4 Case Studies The following examples reproduce ﬁelds from the saved GPT-6-sol and DeepSeek-V4-Flash records. Each example follows one ﬁnding through its group, external research, proposal, implementation report, and evaluation receipts. The displayed ﬁelds are copied in full, without rewriting their values; LaTeX escaping and line wrapping aﬀect presentation only. Other ﬁelds, including long repeated call indexes, are omitted. File names and JSON pointers identify the excerpts. Internal run numbers, join keys, and opaque task identiﬁers are omitted from the reading copy. The underlying complete records and their SHA-256 hashes are retained with the source package. These are the pipelines contemporaneous outputs, including its hypotheses and limitations, rather than retrospective explanations of why task failed. Source-local behavior codes and function names are preserved inside quotations. Model-Speciﬁc Adaptation This appendix describes the changes analyzed in Section 4.4, separating what each mechanism does from its measured eﬀects. The two main models are presented ﬁrst; the earlier GPT-5.6-Terra change is included 32 separately. Evaluation rules and numerical results follow in Appendices and D. B.1 GPT-6-sol The three retained changes improve execution continuity and the evidence returned to the model. Their behavioral locations follow the seed Handbook: session liveness is checked by the Interaction main loop; persisted changes are presented during Observation construction and output truncation; and completionspeciﬁc context is supplied during the Completion conﬁrmation handshake. Completion-claim context. When the agent declares completion, the conﬁrmation message includes evidence of the work performed earlier in the run, rather than only an idle terminal prompt. This modiﬁcation targets the Completion conﬁrmation handshake, supported by observation construction and the recorded execution history. Its implementation setting is completion_claim_context. Persisted workspace feedback. The harness presents changes actually written to ﬁles as workspace diﬀ. The feedback is grounded in persisted ﬁle contents rather than terminal echo, giving the agent view of what changed. Its primary behavioral location is Observation construction and output truncation, with ﬁle inspection supplying the underlying evidence. Its setting is persisted_workspace_diff. Session-loss recovery. When the terminal session disappears, the harness recovers the session and informs the agent of the resulting state loss. This changes the Interaction main loops handling of session liveness, with tmux session operations and observation construction supporting recovery and its feedback. Its setting is single_session_loss_recovery. B.2 DeepSeek-V4-Flash In the seed harness, the ﬁrst completion declaration requests conﬁrmation, and second consecutive declaration permits termination. The four adopted modiﬁcations add checks to this handshake. In Figures 2 and 3, SE denotes structured evidence, DI designated invocation, OO observed operand, and IR independent reading. The corresponding behaviors are detailed below. Each check can withhold completion at most once per run, providing bounded opportunity for correction rather than enforcing an indeﬁnitely repeated veriﬁcation requirement. Primary and supporting stages. The primary stage is where modiﬁcation changes harness decision or action; supporting stages acquire its inputs or maintain the required state. For example, designatedinvocation veriﬁcation reads command history recorded during dispatch but changes the completion decision during the handshake. All four modiﬁcations therefore target Completion conﬁrmation handshake, with their supporting stages listed in Table 2. Executable completion veriﬁcation (SE). The model supplies veriﬁcation command and its expected exit code in the completion declaration. The harness executes the command and compares its exit code with the expected value. match permits this check to release completion; missing ﬁelds, execution failure, or mismatch produce one request to continue working. This makes the models completion evidence executable by the harness, while preserving the bounded withholding rule. Designated-invocation veriﬁcation (DI). When task explicitly speciﬁes an invocation, the harness checks whether it appears in the dispatched-command history. It conservatively extracts the interpreter, script, and arguments from the task instruction, and accommodates absolute paths and relative script paths after directory change through basename matching. The check triggers only when an alternative invocation has been observed but the designated invocation has not. It then requests that the model execute the speciﬁed invocation before conﬁrming completion again.

On the second completion declaration, the harness executes the supplied veriﬁcation command through the sessions environment interface, with 30-second probe limit. The check compares an observed integer exit code with the expected value and records successful match as well as withholding decision. Missing evidence, non-integer result, or mismatch can withhold completion once. If the sandbox call raises an exception, this check fails open, so the probe exception does not itself turn into task failure. Independent-reading corroboration (IR). This check uses existing execution history rather than launching another command. It relates dispatched commands, normalized reading-method signatures, input objects, and values extracted from subsequent observations. If reading used to support completion is backed by only one method, the harness requests diﬀerent form of inspection or second independent reading method. Repeating the same method is not treated as independent corroboration. Implementation boundaries. Executable completion veriﬁcation and completion-outcome observation are separate checks and can execute the same veriﬁcation command twice. Their eﬀects are therefore overlapping. Independent-reading corroboration primarily detects reliance on single reading method: the current evidence-set construction makes the separate conﬂicting-readings branch largely unreachable. We consequently do not describe it as general consistency checker. These are implementation boundaries, not estimates of the individual mechanisms causal contributions. sections.content: This appendix supplements Section 4.1 with scoring, baseline, and version-reporting rules. Numerical results follow in Appendix D. 34 C.1 Repeated Evaluation The default = 4 gives 400 trial slots for TBH and 356 for TB2.1. The metrics in Section 4.1 require complete grid. Passes score 1; task failures and completed runtime failures with valid records score 0, retaining their harness, infrastructure, or unknown-error classiﬁcation. Missing, cancelled, or identity-mismatched measurements are and cannot be dropped to make an incomplete grid valid. Blank table entries mean unreported results, not failures. Aggregate outcome proportions do not identify which initially stable tasks regressed; paired per-task outcomes are needed. C.2 Comparison Protocol Before evaluating candidate, the policy speciﬁes the comparison baseline. For stage on task set S, it selects either historical reference runs or newly measured incumbent control: ( bp B(S) = bp(RtS), bp(Ht; S, rs), bs = historical, bs = fresh. The controller defaults to historical reuse; fresh controls are optional. Historical source identity does not establish unchanged service or environment conditions, so baseline provenance remains part of the evaluation record. Adoption requires valid, complete full evaluation with aggregate pass rate above the declared baseline. Previously stable tasks may regress despite an overall gain, so reliability is reported separately from the adoption score. C.3 Result Reporting The main comparison, cumulative curves, and transfer experiment refer to explicitly identiﬁed harness versions. On DeepSeek-V4-Flash, TBH uses the ﬁnal four-mechanism version (+ IR). Table 1 and Figure 6 report the best observed TB2.1 three-mechanism version (+ OO), selected by its TB2.1 score. This is distinct from directly transferring the ﬁnal version selected on TBH. The full sequence in Appendix D.2 keeps both versions visible. The seeds TBH result is 227/400 passes (56.75%), with 37 all-success, 34 ﬂipping, and 29 all-failure tasks. For the ﬁrst three non-base TB2.1 versions, controller-timeout slots were rerun and merged with the other results; the ﬁnal version uses complete rerun. These diﬀerences in evaluation assembly are retained when interpreting the cumulative sequence. The curves measure combined harness versions rather than isolated causal eﬀects of individual mechanisms.

sections.title: E Scope and Limitations
sections.content: Execution evidence and analysis coverage. Successful runs provide references for failure analysis, but diﬀerences may also reﬂect sampling, environment variation, or task diﬃculty. Discovery from traceable ﬂipping tasks excludes consistently failing tasks and failures before recording. The monitor covers selected boundaries, and the Handbook may omit behavior or become stale. Neither source establishes causality. Candidate changes and regression risks. External designs may require unavailable interfaces or signals. Behavioral checks cover ﬁnite cases, while combined-candidate evaluation does not isolate individual mechanisms. Aggregate-score adoption can retain changes that harm previously stable tasks; aggregate outcome proportions cannot quantify these regressions without per-task comparisons. Evaluation and transfer. Repeated development-set selection can exploit noise, and historical baselines are sensitive to service or environment drift. Retained-score trends therefore require independent evaluation. The reporting protocol in Appendix C.3 distinguishes target-selected versions from frozen ﬁnal-version transfer. 37 Cross-model swapping shows model dependence for the tested harnesses, without ruling out transfer of individual mechanisms between other models. Scope and resource costs. Other harnesses require compatible monitoring, behavioral mappings, and evaluation adapters. Long runs, external research, and repeated evaluation incur inference and storage costs; conﬁgured concurrency is not measured speedup. LLMCarbon motivates broader resource accounting [39], but emissions are not measured here. The loop keeps model weights ﬁxed and does not learn its outer controller. Training-side methods, including work on asynchronous policy mismatch [40], are complementary directions for future study.
